messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Doctor
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Vignette:
Raúl, a 67-year-old Latin American physician who lived alone, had built his adult life around steadiness, competence, and the quiet routines of medical work, and it was precisely that identity that made the crisis with his son so devastatingly disorganizing. Years earlier, his son had become critically ill, and the illness had moved through their family life with the brutal unpredictability of a medical emergency that could not be held at bay by training or experience. Raúl remembered being in the hospital with him, moving between the bedside, the corridor, and conversations that seemed to end before they had fully begun. Even now, he could recall only fragments of that period: the harsh fluorescent light, the tension in the room, the look on his son’s face, the feeling that the air itself had become heavy and unreal. When he tried to describe what happened, he could not make it into a clear account. He knew the broad facts, but the details felt broken apart, as if the middle of the story had gone missing. At times he could say only that “something terrible happened,” because the words for the sequence of events would not come to him, and the memories arrived in pieces rather than a coherent narrative.

In the months that followed, Raúl began trying hard not to think about the illness or the time in the hospital. He found that even a brief thought about it could pull him back into the same state of dread, so he made a habit of pushing the memories away. He kept his mind occupied all the time, filling the day with work, reading, errands, and anything that required concentration. As a doctor, he was surrounded by reminders of illness, but he learned to move quickly past any conversation, case, or detail that might let his thoughts drift toward his son’s experience. When the memory threatened to surface, he would redirect himself immediately, as if mental busyness might hold the whole thing at a safe distance. This had become so routine that his days were now organized around staying ahead of the moment when he might have to remember.

Yet the memory did not remain politely contained. At times, something abrupt would catch him off guard, and he would suddenly feel as if he were back there again. A sound, a medical phrase, or the atmosphere of an exam room could make him feel and react for a moment as though the crisis were happening in real time. In those moments, he became intensely watchful, scanning the room and his own body with a kind of alarm that he found exhausting. He was on guard in a way that he recognized as excessive but could not fully turn off. Even in ordinary settings, he kept alert for signs that something was about to go wrong. What frightened him most was not only the intensity of these episodes but the sense that his mind could be pulled so easily into the past without warning, leaving him abruptly disoriented and exposed.

Raúl also carried strong negative emotions that he did not experience as fleeting. He described fear that could rise suddenly, alongside horror, anger, and guilt that lingered after the event and seemed to return whenever the illness came to mind. Part of him remained angry at how powerless he had felt, and part of him felt guilty for not being able to prevent his son’s suffering. Those feelings were not neatly ordered; they arrived together, often during quiet moments when there was no one to interrupt him. He would then feel as though he should have been stronger, more useful, or more able to protect his child, even though he knew rationally that the illness had not been in his control.

Over time, these reactions changed how he lived. Because thinking about the event was so distressing, he increasingly arranged his life around staying busy, and his home and work routines reflected that need to avoid even a moment of stillness. His occupation as a doctor meant he remained in environments where illness, urgency, and monitoring were part of daily life, and that could place him suddenly face to face with reminders he had not planned for. In the clinic or hospital, he could become sharply alert when a patient’s condition resembled the kinds of uncertainty he had lived through with his son. Although he remained functional and continued working, he noticed that this constant readiness left him depleted and uneasy.

What finally brought Raúl to seek help was the growing sense that these experiences were no longer just part of a painful past but were intruding into the present with enough force that he could not simply outwork them. He came because he was tired of having to keep his mind occupied all the time, tired of the fragments that would appear without warning, and tired of feeling that the story of his son’s illness could never be fully told. He hoped for a way to remember without being overwhelmed, and he feared that, without help, he would continue living as though he were always bracing for the next recurrence of the same unbearable moment.
